name: Lusinga or Chula
confidence_why: Nothing describes Singa stress directly: the only statement is Johnston's 1904 blanket printing convention that unmarked words in all fifty of his Uganda vocabularies carry penultimate accent, applied to Hobley's 1902 unmarked Singa wordlist (where Johnston marks one item on the antepenult, Mwanámtu), and no grammar or phonology of this extinct language exists.

' shows where the accent falls: in the absence of any mark the accent falls on the penultimate syllable. A long vowel is marked by -, and nasalisation by ~. When t, and k or other terminal consonants are thus crossed through it means they are only half pronounced. Many terminal consonants in Acholi, Bari, and other Nilotic tongues are not exploded ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Johnston's blanket transcription rule for all the vocabularies in the volume: a word carries an accent mark only when the accent is not penultimate; unmarked words are accented on the penultimate syllable. The Lusinga (Singa) wordlist on pp. 993-1001 has no accent marks on any form, so under his convention every recorded Singa word is penult-accented. This is an implication of a general orthographic convention (applied equally to Somali, Masai, Nilotic and Bantu lists), not an observation made about Singa; Johnston 1919 vol. 1 p. 41 restates it as 'the prevailing rule in Bantu'.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Singa (no accent-marked forms in the Lusinga column). Generically, the mark ' would flag non-penultimate accent; Johnston 1919 p. 41 adds that monosyllables are not accented 'unless uttered with vehemence'.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation-form wordlist items (nouns mostly with class prefix, some phrases). No Singa-specific phonological description exists; the two wordlists (Hobley 1902, Johnston 1904) are the entire documentation of the language and Hobley's has no pronunciation key at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Singa = 'Lusinga or Chula' of Hobley 1902 and Johnston 1904 (spoken by the Awa-Ware / Wa-Chula, 'people of the island', on Lusinga [Rusinga] and Lufangano [Rufangano] islands at the mouth of Kavirondo/Winam Gulf, Kenya, Homa Bay County; Wikipedia's 'Uganda' is wrong). Johnston 1919 treats it as dialect 5b of Luwanga 'much mixed with Lu-ganda and Ku-kerebe'; Glottolog and Maho (JE406) treat it as a distinct North Nyanza language. It is not the Suba (Olusuba, JE403) now spoken on Rusinga Island, and Koné 1991 in the Glottolog list ('verbes Dóno et Sínga du Jula') is a false hit on Jula (Côte d'Ivoire).

sources.note: Blanket Bantu convention, p. 41: 'The accent or pitch of the voice is indicated by \'. This is so normally and frequently on the penultimate syllable that the accent is only employed when an exception to the prevailing rule in Bantu transfers the voice-pitch to the first, last, or other syllable than the penultimate. Monosyllables are not accented unless uttered with vehemence.' Singa itself appears only as dialect 5b of Luwanga ('Lu-singa or Cula.. is a dialect of Lu-wanga much mixed with Lu-ganda and Ku-kerebe words', p. 73 fn.) in the comparative word tables; nothing Singa-specific on acce…

sources.citation: Johnston, Harry H. 1904. The Uganda Protectorate, vol. 2. London: Hutchinson. 'Orthography employed in these vocabularies' p. 901; vocabulary set 48 'Lusinga or Chula' pp. 993-1001.
sources.note: Only a blanket transcription convention on p. 901 covering all 50 vocabularies in the volume (Somali, Masai, Nilotic and Bantu alike): "' shows where the accent falls: in the absence of any mark the accent falls on the penultimate syllable." The Lusinga column (checked on the p. 996 page scan) carries no accent marks at all, only macrons for long vowels (Mūtwe, Endūi), so by the convention every Lusinga word is implicitly penult-accented; no Singa-specific remark on accent anywhere.
